title: Gideon and the Tide
premise: Jonah Oyelaran has spent ten years raising her son in the coastal town of Bellhaven, hiding behind the counter of her bookshop and an anonymous pen-pal letter exchange she runs for the town festival. When a clerical error pairs her with Gideon Marsh, the man whose testimony helped take her late husband's family business—and her old life—apart, she must decide whether to reveal herself or let the correspondence deepen. As letters become confidences and confidences become love, the truth of her identity surfaces at the worst possible moment, on the festival's final night. Jonah must choose between the safe invisibility she built and a man willing to stay past the last train, past his own guilt, for her.
about_author: T. M. Marchetti is the pen name of a former small-town bookseller who now writes romance about people who rebuild their lives one careful step at a time. She lives near the sea with her family and an unreasonable number of unread paperbacks.

chapters.title: The Last Train Schedule
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Ten years after fleeing scandal in the city, Jonah runs the bookshop and secretly administers Bellhaven's anonymous pen-pal exchange, a tradition she loves precisely because no one knows her. Her son Teo asks why she never writes her own letter. Emotional beat: the ache of a life built entirely around safety.

chapters.title: A Clerical Error
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon, the town's new ferry engineer, volunteers for the pen-pal program to feel less like an outsider. A filing mistake pairs him with a correspondent who is sharp, guarded, and oddly familiar in her phrasing. He writes anyway. Emotional beat: tentative hope from a man carrying his own quiet shame.

chapters.title: What We Don't Sign
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah realizes the handwriting on the reply is Gideon Marsh's—the man whose testimony destroyed her in-laws' business and, in her grief-blurred memory, her marriage. She nearly burns the letter, but his words are gentle in a way she never expected. Emotional beat: fury and curiosity colliding; she writes back anonymously, telling herself it's reconnaissance.

chapters.title: Small Safe Steps
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The letters deepen while their real-life encounters stay brittle: he fixes the shop's leaking roof; she serves him coffee without a smile. Teo befriends Gideon at the harbor, unaware. Emotional beat: the gap between who they are on paper and in person widens until it aches.

chapters.title: The Letter She Kept
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Gideon's letter confesses his testimony was coerced by a developer's lawyers, that he's spent years trying to make it right, and that he came to Bellhaven chasing the family he wronged. Jonah realizes he doesn't know she's the widow. Emotional beat: her hatred cracks into something dangerously like understanding.

chapters.title: Low Tide
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon figures out his correspondent is Jonah—a phrase in her letters echoes the bookshop's chalkboard. He says nothing, terrified of losing the one honest connection he has. Meanwhile Jonah, emboldened, nearly tells him the truth in person and fails. Emotional beat: two people circling the same secret, each protecting the other from it.

chapters.title: Everything the Tide Returns
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The developer returns to Bellhaven, and Gideon publicly testifies against him—this time for Jonah's in-laws, restoring the family name. Jonah watches from the back of the hall, realizing he's been fighting for her all along without knowing it. Emotional beat: gratitude so sharp it feels like grief; she knows she must now confess her deception.

chapters.title: The Name at the Bottom
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the festival's opening night, Jonah signs her final anonymous letter with her real name and leaves it in his mailbox, then hides in the shop, ready to lose him. Gideon arrives soaked from the rain, furious not at her identity but that she thought he'd leave. They argue, break, and almost kiss—then the truth of his earlier silence comes out. Emotional beat: the climactic rupture; both secrets laid bare, trust in pieces.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Gideon, humiliated, packs for the last train out. Teo, who has pieced it together, gives Jonah his mother's old letter—the very first anonymous one she wrote years ago, signed with a phrase Gideon quoted back to her in chapter five. She runs for the station through the festival crowd. Emotional beat: the choice between invisibility and belonging made with her feet.

chapters.title: What the Festival Keeps
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah reaches the platform as the last train pulls away—Gideon never boarded; he's standing on the emptying street holding her letter. They meet in the middle of the shuttered festival, and he asks to stay, not for a night, but for good. Epilogue beat: spring, the bookshop, a new pen-pal box with two names signed side by side. Emotional beat: home is a person who stays.
